title: Seventy-two, divided by the rate
body: Money growing at a constant rate takes roughly 72 divided by the percentage rate to double. At 8% a year that gives nine years, against an exact 9.01. At 6% it predicts twelve years against 11.90. The shortcut works because doubling time is ln(2)/ln(1+r), and ln(1+r) tracks r closely at small rates. Accuracy is best between roughly 5% and 12%.
prompt: How can you estimate a doubling time from a growth rate without a calculator?
answer: Divide 72 by the rate expressed as a percentage. At 8% a year that gives nine years against an exact 9.01, and the approximation is most accurate for rates roughly between 5% and 12%.

title: Ten million, or a penny that doubles
body: Someone offers you a choice, and you must pick before seeing it play out. Option A is ten million dollars, handed over today. Option B is one cent today, two cents tomorrow, four the day after, doubling every day for thirty days, and you keep every payment. No inflation, no taxes, no interest on money already received. Most people take the ten million without doing any arithmetic.
prompt: Which is worth more: ten million dollars now, or a penny that doubles daily for thirty days with every payment kept?
answer: The doubling penny, by about $737,000. The payments run 1, 2, 4 and so on up to 2^29 cents, and a sum of doubling terms equals twice the last term minus one, here 2^30 - 1 cents, or $10,737,418.23. More than half the total arrives on the final two days alone.

title: Why discounting is not about inflation
body: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year because today's dollar can be invested and earn a return. Discounting runs that logic backwards. A payment of $1,000 due in three years, at a 6% annual rate, is worth 1000 divided by 1.06 cubed, about $840, today. The discount rate is not a guess about inflation. At root it is the return the money could otherwise earn.
prompt: Why is a future payment worth less than the same nominal amount today, and how is the discount computed?
answer: Because money held today can be invested and earn a return, so it grows into a larger sum by the future date. Discounting divides the future payment by (1 + r) raised to the number of periods: $1,000 due in three years at 6% is worth about $840 now.

title: Infinite payments, finite value
body: A perpetuity pays a fixed amount forever, so it sounds as though it should be worth infinitely much. Its present value is just the payment divided by the discount rate. A bond paying 100 pounds a year forever, discounted at 5%, is worth 2,000 pounds. Each more distant payment is discounted more heavily than the last, so the discounted amounts shrink geometrically and the infinite sum converges. Britain issued exactly this instrument, called consols, and redeemed the last of them in 2015.
prompt: How can a stream of payments that never ends have a finite present value?
answer: Its present value is the periodic payment divided by the discount rate, so 100 pounds a year at 5% is worth 2,000 pounds. The total is finite because each successive payment is discounted more heavily, so the discounted payments shrink geometrically and the series converges.

title: The million-dollar prize that isn't
body: A lottery advertises a one million dollar prize. The fine print says it is paid as $50,000 at the end of each year for twenty years, not as a lump sum. You can borrow and lend freely at 5% a year. Ignore taxes and inflation. Twenty payments of fifty thousand does add up to a million, so the arithmetic on the poster is correct. It is not what the prize is worth to you today.
prompt: A prize of $50,000 a year for twenty years is advertised as $1,000,000. What is it actually worth today at a 5% discount rate?
answer: About $623,000. Each payment is divided by 1.05 raised to the year it arrives, and the sum gives an annuity factor of about 12.46, times $50,000. The advertised million adds dollars from twenty different years as though they were the same good, and they are not.

title: Nominal rates versus real rates
body: The interest rate your bank quotes is nominal. What matters for purchasing power is the real rate, roughly the nominal rate minus inflation. Earn 5% on a deposit while prices rise 3%, and you are only about 2% richer in goods. The exact Fisher relation gives 1.94% here, close enough that the subtraction shortcut is fine at low rates. Real rates can be negative, and often have been.
prompt: Your deposit pays 5% while prices rise 3%. How much better off are you, and what is that figure called?
answer: About 2% better off in goods, which is the real interest rate as against the 5% nominal rate the bank quotes. The exact Fisher relation gives 1.94%, so subtracting inflation from the nominal rate is a good approximation at low rates.

title: Why bond prices and yields move opposite
body: A bond's coupon payments are fixed when it is issued. If market rates rise afterwards, newly issued bonds pay more, so nobody will pay full price for the old one. Its price falls until the return a buyer earns from holding it to maturity matches what new bonds offer. That return is the yield, so price and yield are two ways of quoting the same thing.
prompt: Why do a bond's price and its yield always move in opposite directions?
answer: Because the bond's coupon payments are fixed, the only thing that can adjust when market rates change is the price. A lower price means a buyer earns a higher return on the same fixed cash flows, and that higher return is exactly what a higher yield means.

title: How far away a bond's money sits
body: Duration measures how far in the future a bond's cash flows sit, weighting each payment by its share of the bond's present value. It doubles as a sensitivity measure: a bond with duration near seven falls roughly 7% in price when yields rise by one percentage point. A zero-coupon bond pays only at maturity, so its duration equals its maturity. Coupon bonds return some cash earlier, which pulls the weighted average in.
prompt: What does a bond's duration measure, and what does a duration near seven imply about its price sensitivity?
answer: Duration is the present-value-weighted average time until a bond's cash flows arrive, and it approximates interest-rate sensitivity. A duration near seven means the price falls roughly 7% if yields rise by one percentage point.

title: Same maturity, different damage
body: Two bonds both mature in exactly ten years and both currently yield 5%. Bond A is a zero-coupon bond, paying nothing at all until a single lump sum at maturity. Bond B pays a 10% annual coupon and then its face value. Market yields suddenly rise from 5% to 6% for both. Same issuer, same maturity, same yield move, yet the two prices do not fall by the same percentage.
prompt: Two ten-year bonds, one zero-coupon and one with a 10% coupon, both yield 5%. Which loses more when yields rise to 6%, and why?
answer: The zero-coupon bond, falling about 9.0% against about 6.6% for the coupon bond. The zero's entire payment sits ten years out, so its present-value-weighted average payment date is the full ten years. The coupon bond returns cash along the way, pulling that average in to roughly seven years and blunting its rate sensitivity.

title: What an inversion does and does not tell you
body: The yield curve plots government bond yields against maturity. It usually slopes upward, since lenders want more compensation for tying money up longer. Occasionally it inverts, with short yields above long ones, which implies markets expect short rates to fall. In the United States an inversion has preceded every recession since the 1960s, with at least one false alarm. Economists dispute what to make of that: whether inversion causes anything, merely reflects expectations, or is a regularity that could break.
prompt: What is an inverted yield curve, and how confident should you be in what it predicts?
answer: An inversion means short-maturity government yields exceed long-maturity ones, implying markets expect short rates to fall. In the US it has preceded every recession since the 1960s with at least one false alarm, but economists disagree over whether it is causal, merely reflects expectations, or is a regularity that could break.

title: The Gordon growth model
body: A share is a claim on a company's future cash to shareholders, so its value is those payments discounted back to today. The Gordon growth version compresses this into one line. If a stock pays a dividend D next year, growing forever at rate g, and investors require return r, the value is D divided by (r minus g). It only works when r exceeds g.
prompt: How does the Gordon growth model value a share, and what is its key restriction?
answer: It values the share as next year's dividend divided by the required return minus the perpetual growth rate, or D/(r - g). The model requires r to exceed g, and the answer is extremely sensitive to small changes in either input.

title: A P/E ratio is a question, not an answer
body: A price-to-earnings ratio is the share price divided by earnings per share. A stock at $50 earning $2.50 a share has a P/E of 20, meaning buyers pay twenty dollars per dollar of current annual profit. It is not a verdict. A high P/E can mean investors expect fast earnings growth, or that the stock is expensive, or that earnings are temporarily depressed, and the ratio cannot tell you which.
prompt: What does a price-to-earnings ratio measure, and why can't a high P/E alone tell you a stock is overpriced?
answer: It is the share price divided by earnings per share, the price paid per dollar of current annual profit. A high P/E is ambiguous: it can reflect expected earnings growth, genuine overvaluation, or temporarily depressed earnings, and the ratio alone cannot distinguish between them.

title: What the bid-ask spread pays for
body: At any moment a market has two prices: the bid, the highest price someone will pay, and the ask, the lowest price someone will sell at. The gap between them is the spread, and it is what trading immediately costs you, since you buy at the ask and sell at the bid. It compensates whoever supplies that immediacy for three things: processing the order, holding inventory that may move against them, and trading against someone better informed.
prompt: Trading in and straight back out loses you money even if the price never moves. What have you paid, and what does it buy?
answer: You have paid the bid-ask spread, the gap between the highest price a buyer will pay and the lowest a seller will accept. It compensates the liquidity provider for order-processing costs, inventory risk, and the risk of trading against someone better informed.

title: Market orders and limit orders trade one certainty for another
body: A market order says trade now, at whatever price is available. A limit order says trade only at my price or better, and wait. The trade-off is exact. A market order buys certainty of execution and pays the spread. A limit order earns the spread but may never fill, and worse, it tends to fill precisely when the price is moving through it. You are choosing which uncertainty to bear: price, or execution.
prompt: You can trade now at the market price or name your price and wait. What are you giving up in each case?
answer: A market order guarantees execution but not price, and pays the spread. A limit order fixes the price but not whether it executes, and earns the spread. The choice is which uncertainty to accept, with limit orders also bearing the risk of filling only when informed traders push the price through them.

title: The risk diversification cannot touch
body: Hold one company's stock and you carry two kinds of risk: things that happen only to that firm, such as a fire or a lawsuit or a bad chief executive, and things that hit every firm at once, like a recession or a rate shock. Own fifty firms and the firm-specific shocks largely cancel, since some go badly and some go well. The economy-wide shocks do not cancel, because they strike everything together.
prompt: Which kind of risk does diversification remove, and which does it leave behind?
answer: It removes idiosyncratic, firm-specific risk, because largely independent shocks across many holdings tend to cancel out. It cannot remove systematic risk: shocks like recessions or interest rate moves that hit every holding at the same time.

title: Diversification runs on correlation, not on counting
body: Take two assets, each with a 20% standard deviation of returns, and split your money evenly between them. If the two are uncorrelated, the portfolio's standard deviation drops to about 14%. If they move perfectly together, it stays at 20% and you have gained nothing. Owning thirty stocks in one industry is much closer to the second case. Correlations, not the number of names on the statement, decide how much risk disappears.
prompt: Why does diversification depend on correlation rather than on the number of holdings?
answer: Because risk falls only when shocks cancel, which requires holdings that do not move together. Two 20%-volatility assets split evenly give about 14% volatility if uncorrelated, but still 20% if perfectly correlated, so thirty highly correlated stocks diversify very little.

title: A call option buys an asymmetry
body: A call option gives you the right, not the obligation, to buy an asset at a fixed strike price. If the asset ends above the strike you exercise and pocket the difference. Below it you walk away and lose only what you paid. Buy a $100-strike call for $5: at $130 you net $25, and at $60 you lose $5, not $40. That bent payoff, floored on one side and open on the other, is what the premium buys.
prompt: Buying a $100-strike call for $5, you lose $5 if the stock falls to $60 but make $25 if it rises to $130. What are you actually paying for?
answer: An asymmetry. The option is a right rather than an obligation, so you exercise only when doing so pays, which caps your loss at the premium while leaving gains open above the strike. The premium buys that bent payoff, not a prediction about direction.

title: Why volatility makes an option worth more
body: An option's price usually exceeds what you would get from exercising it right now. The extra is time value, and it grows with how long is left and how much the underlying is expected to move. Volatility helps the holder because the downside is capped at the premium while the upside is not, so a wider range of outcomes only widens the profitable tail. Implied volatility inverts this: it is the volatility that makes a pricing model reproduce the option's market price.
prompt: Why does more expected volatility raise an option's price, and what is implied volatility?
answer: Because the holder's loss is capped at the premium while the gain is not, so a wider distribution of outcomes extends only the profitable tail. Implied volatility is the volatility input that makes a pricing model output the option's observed market price.

title: The call, the put, and the free lunch
body: A stock trades at $100 and pays no dividends. A European call struck at $100 and expiring in one year trades at $8. A European put with the same strike and expiry trades at $2. You can borrow or lend at 5% a year, and there are no transaction costs. Holding the stock, plus that put, minus that call, guarantees you exactly $100 in a year no matter where the stock ends up.
prompt: A no-dividend stock is at $100; a one-year $100 call trades at $8 and the matching put at $2, with a 5% rate. Where is the arbitrage?
answer: Sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock, and borrow $95.24, the present value of $100. That nets $1.24 today, and the position settles at exactly zero, since the guaranteed $100 repays the loan grown to $100. Parity requires call minus put to equal $4.76, but the market prices that difference at $6, so the call is dear relative to the put.

title: Three currencies that do not agree
body: Three quotes are live at the same instant at three banks, all with zero fees and unlimited size. One dollar buys 0.90 euros. One euro buys 160 yen. One dollar buys 150 yen. You hold $1,000 and may convert in any sequence you like, so long as you end back in dollars. These three rates are not mutually consistent, and the inconsistency is worth money to whoever works out which way around to trade.
prompt: Given $1 = €0.90, €1 = ¥160, and $1 = ¥150, how do you turn $1,000 into a risk-free profit?
answer: Go dollars to yen to euros to dollars: $1,000 buys ¥150,000, which buys €937.50, which buys about $1,041.67, a risk-free gain of roughly $41.67. The key step is the implied cross rate. Routed through euros a dollar is worth only ¥144, but the direct quote gives ¥150, so buy yen directly and unwind back through euros.

title: Where a bank loan's money comes from
body: The textbook story is that banks lend out the deposits savers bring in. The Bank of England's own account is different. When a bank makes a loan it simultaneously credits the borrower's account with a brand-new deposit, and no pre-existing money moves from anyone. That deposit is new money in the economy, and it is destroyed again when the loan is repaid. What limits the process is not a stock of reserves but profitability, credit risk, capital requirements, and the policy rate.
prompt: According to the Bank of England, where does the money come from when a commercial bank makes a loan?
answer: The bank creates it, crediting the borrower's account with a new deposit at the moment the loan is made, rather than lending out money savers deposited first. That deposit is new money and is destroyed when the loan is repaid; lending is limited by profitability, credit risk, capital rules, and the policy rate.

title: Borrow short, lend long, and hope
body: A bank borrows short and lends long. Depositors can withdraw today, while the mortgages and business loans on the other side of the balance sheet take years to mature and cannot be sold quickly at full value. This maturity transformation is genuinely useful, since it lets illiquid projects be funded by people who want liquidity. It is also structurally fragile. If enough depositors demand their money at once, a bank whose loans are perfectly good still fails.
prompt: What is maturity transformation, and why does it make even a solvent bank fragile?
answer: A bank funds long-term, illiquid loans with deposits that can be withdrawn on demand. If enough depositors withdraw at once it cannot liquidate those assets quickly at full value, so it fails even though its loans are sound. That is the logic deposit insurance exists to break.

title: How a central bank actually sets the rate
body: A central bank does not decree the interest rate you pay. It controls the rate at the very short end and lets markets do the rest. Before 2008 the Federal Reserve kept bank reserves scarce and nudged the overnight rate by buying and selling small quantities of securities. Since then it has kept reserves abundant and steers the rate mainly by paying interest on reserves, which sets a floor a bank has little reason to lend below.
prompt: How does a central bank with abundant reserves steer the short-term interest rate?
answer: It pays interest on reserves, which sets a floor: a bank has little reason to lend overnight below what it can earn risk-free at the central bank. The Federal Reserve moved to this approach after 2008, replacing the pre-crisis method of keeping reserves scarce and adjusting their quantity.

title: Quantitative easing: clear mechanism, disputed effect
body: In quantitative easing a central bank creates reserves and uses them to buy longer-dated bonds. Mechanically this swaps a long, duration-heavy asset for a short, safe one, shrinking the interest rate risk private investors must hold between them. It also signals that policy rates will stay low. How much it actually moved output and inflation is genuinely disputed.
prompt: What does quantitative easing do mechanically, and how settled are its macroeconomic effects?
answer: A central bank creates reserves to buy longer-dated bonds, which removes interest rate risk from private portfolios and signals that policy rates will stay low, both of which push long-term yields down. Its effect on output and inflation is genuinely disputed, with credible estimates spanning from substantial to near zero.

title: Substitution bias in a price index
body: A consumer price index prices a fixed basket of goods each month and reports how much that basket's cost changed. The trouble is that people substitute. When beef gets expensive they buy more chicken, so a fixed basket overstates what it actually costs them to stay equally well off. The 1996 Boskin Commission put total US CPI overstatement at around 1.1 percentage points a year. The statistical agency has since made changes, including a chained index that lets the basket adjust.
prompt: What is substitution bias in a consumer price index, and roughly how large did the Boskin Commission put total US CPI bias?
answer: A fixed basket ignores that consumers switch toward goods that have become relatively cheaper, so it overstates the cost of maintaining the same standard of living. The 1996 Boskin Commission estimated total US CPI overstatement at roughly 1.1 percentage points a year.

title: The disagreement economists are best known for
body: The competitive labor model predicts that a wage floor set above the market rate reduces employment. The monopsony model, where employers have wage-setting power, predicts a moderate floor can raise both wages and employment. Both are respectable theory. Card and Krueger's 1994 study of New Jersey fast food found no job losses, while Neumark and Wascher contested the data and found some. Decades of studies have not settled it.
prompt: Why do economists disagree about whether a minimum wage reduces employment?
answer: Because two credible models predict opposite things. The competitive model implies job losses, while the monopsony model allows a moderate floor to raise employment, and the empirical evidence is genuinely mixed, from Card and Krueger's null result to Neumark and Wascher's contrary findings. The effect likely depends on the floor's height relative to local wages.

title: Being worse at everything and still gaining from trade
body: Suppose one country is better at making both cloth and wine than another. It still gains by specializing. What matters is not who is better in absolute terms but what each must give up. If a barrel of wine costs the first country two bolts of cloth and costs the second only one, the second should make the wine, whatever its absolute productivity. Trading at any rate between those two opportunity costs leaves both consuming more of both goods.
prompt: Why can a country that is worse at producing everything still gain from trade?
answer: Because gains come from comparative, not absolute, advantage. Each country should specialize where its opportunity cost, meaning what it gives up to make a good, is lower. Trading at a rate between the two countries' opportunity costs leaves both consuming more than they could produce on their own.

title: What economists agree and disagree about on trade
body: Economists agree nearly unanimously that trade raises a country's total income, which follows from comparative advantage. The disagreement is everything downstream. Standard theory says trade also redistributes, hurting whoever competes with imports, and assumes those workers move into other jobs reasonably fast. Research on the China shock found that in hard-hit American regions they largely did not, with employment and wages staying depressed for years.
prompt: What do economists broadly agree on about trade, and what is genuinely disputed?
answer: There is near-consensus that trade raises aggregate income through comparative advantage. The dispute is about distribution and adjustment: how large and persistent the losses to import-competing workers and regions are, with China shock research finding adjustment far slower than standard models assume.

title: Why cartels fall apart
body: A cartel agrees to restrict output so that prices stay high. The agreement is valuable to every member, and it is unstable for exactly that reason. Once the others are holding production back the price is high, so the profitable move for you is to quietly produce more and sell it at that high price. Every member faces the same incentive, so cheating spreads and the price sags.
prompt: Why are cartel agreements structurally unstable?
answer: Because each member's individually best move is to defect: with the others restricting output and holding the price up, quietly producing extra is profitable regardless of what anyone else does. That is a prisoner's dilemma, so the cooperative outcome tends to unravel.

title: Two firms, and the price collapses anyway
body: Two firms sell an identical product. Each can produce any quantity at a constant cost of $10 per unit, with no capacity limit. They post prices simultaneously, once, and cannot communicate. Every customer buys from whichever firm is cheaper, and a tie splits the market evenly. Intuition says two firms is nearly a monopoly, so prices should settle well above cost.
prompt: Two firms with identical $10 unit costs simultaneously post prices for an identical good and customers buy the cheaper. What is the equilibrium price?
answer: Both price at $10, their marginal cost, and earn zero profit. The key step is that at any common price above cost either firm can shade its price by a penny and capture the whole market rather than half of it. No price above $10 survives, and no firm will price below cost, so two firms suffice for the competitive outcome.

title: The winner pays too much
body: Ten oil companies bid for a drilling tract in a sealed auction. The highest bid wins and pays its bid. The tract's true value is the same for all of them, but nobody knows what it is. Each company's geologists produce an unbiased estimate, right on average and as likely to be too high as too low. Every firm bids exactly its own estimate. On average, the winner loses money.
prompt: If every bidder bids their own unbiased estimate of an item's common value, why does the winner tend to lose money?
answer: This is the winner's curse: you win precisely when your estimate was the most optimistic of the ten, so the fact of winning is itself evidence your estimate was too high. Unbiased on average is not unbiased conditional on winning. The fix is to shade your bid below your estimate, by more when there are more bidders or noisier estimates.

title: Losses loom larger than gains
body: People do not treat gains and losses symmetrically. Kahneman and Tversky found that a loss of a given size feels worse than an equal gain feels good, and put the ratio at roughly two to one. It shows up as reluctance to sell a losing position, and as choices flipping when the same outcome is described as a gain rather than a loss. The effect is well established. Its exact size and universality are still argued over.
prompt: What is loss aversion, and how settled is the size of the effect?
answer: It is the finding that a loss weighs more heavily than a gain of the same size, which Kahneman and Tversky estimated at roughly a two-to-one ratio. The phenomenon is well established, but its magnitude and how universally it holds remain actively debated.

title: The money is already gone
body: You have spent $8,000 on a car repair and the car still is not fixed. Another $2,000 might do it, or might not. The $8,000 is gone whichever way you choose, so it should carry zero weight. The only live question is whether $2,000 buys more here than anywhere else. People systematically fail this and escalate, because walking away feels like conceding the earlier money was wasted. It was wasted regardless.
prompt: Why should sunk costs carry no weight in a decision?
answer: Because they are unrecoverable whichever option you pick, so they are identical across the options and cannot distinguish between them. Only future costs and benefits at the margin are relevant, though people systematically escalate commitment instead of ignoring what is already spent.

title: Adverse selection is not moral hazard
body: Two problems get routinely confused. Adverse selection is hidden information before a deal: the sick buy more health insurance, so the pool an insurer actually gets is worse than the population. Moral hazard is hidden action after a deal: once insured, people lock the bike a little less carefully. The distinction is timing and what is hidden, a type versus a behavior, and it dictates the remedy.
prompt: What distinguishes adverse selection from moral hazard?
answer: Adverse selection is hidden information before contracting: the counterparty's type is unknown, so worse risks self-select in. Moral hazard is hidden action after contracting: being covered changes behavior. Screening and signaling address the first; deductibles and monitoring address the second.

title: The market that eats itself
body: Half the used cars for sale are good and half are defective, and only the seller knows which is which. A buyer would pay $10,000 for a good one and $2,000 for a bad one. Owners of good cars will not part with them below $8,000; owners of bad cars will accept anything above $1,000. Buyers cannot inspect, and everyone knows all of these numbers. A risk-neutral buyer starts out offering the average, $6,000.
prompt: With buyers offering $6,000 for a used car equally likely to be good or bad, what happens to this market and why?
answer: It collapses to bad cars only. At $6,000 no good-car owner sells, since they value theirs at $8,000, so only bad cars are offered, and buyers infer this and cut their bid toward $2,000. The key step is that the price determines which sellers turn up, so average quality is not a fixed input but responds to the offer.

title: Why paying a manager in stock only half works
body: A principal-agent problem arises whenever one party acts on behalf of another whose interests differ and whose actions cannot be fully observed. Shareholders want long-run firm value. A manager wants a career, and only she knows how hard she is really working. Paying her in stock is the standard fix and genuinely does tie her outcome to theirs. It also rewards raising the share price by any route at all.
prompt: Shareholders cannot see how hard a manager works, so they pay her in stock. What does that fix, and what does it leave broken?
answer: It fixes the alignment of outcomes, since her wealth now moves with theirs. It leaves the underlying principal-agent problem intact, because it rewards any route to a higher share price, including excessive risk-taking, disclosure timing, or cutting long-horizon investment, rather than genuine value creation.

title: Two Nobel laureates who disagree about prices
body: The efficient market hypothesis holds that asset prices already reflect available information, so public information cannot be used to beat the market reliably. Eugene Fama argued the evidence supports it, pointing out that most active managers underperform simple indexes. Robert Shiller argued that prices swing far more than any news about future dividends can justify. They shared the Nobel in the same year, 2013, which tells you how unsettled it is.
prompt: What does the efficient market hypothesis claim, and why is it considered unsettled?
answer: It claims prices already incorporate available information, so public information cannot reliably be used to beat the market. It is unsettled because Fama's evidence that active managers underperform indexes and Shiller's evidence of excess volatility both have real support. They shared the 2013 Nobel.

title: Costs that never show on a receipt
body: Every choice made under scarcity forecloses alternatives, and its true cost is the best of those forgone options, not the money spent. Spending a Saturday building a deck yourself has a price even if you buy no labor: the most valuable thing you gave up that day. A firm holding cash in a vault forgoes the interest it could have earned. Because this cost leaves no invoice, decisions that look free often are not.
prompt: You spend a free Saturday building a deck yourself and pay nobody. In what sense was it still expensive?
answer: You paid the opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative use of that day, which need not be monetary. Every choice under scarcity forecloses others, so a decision can be costly even when no invoice is issued and no money changes hands.

title: Why the value grows with the crowd
body: For some products, each new user makes the product more valuable to everyone else. A phone network or a marketplace is nearly useless with one user and compelling with millions. This positive feedback can tip a market. Once a product pulls ahead, its growing value attracts still more users, and rivals struggle even if technically better.
prompt: Why can a technically inferior product end up dominating a market and staying there?
answer: A network effect means a product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it, as with phone networks or marketplaces. This positive feedback can tip a market toward a single dominant product and lock users in, so market share need not reflect superior quality.

title: When raising the price lowers the takings
body: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity sold responds to a price change: the percent change in units per one percent change in price. If demand is inelastic, buyers barely cut back when prices rise, so a higher price increases total revenue. If demand is elastic, buyers flee, and a price rise lowers revenue while a cut raises it. A seller's revenue-maximizing move depends entirely on which regime it is in.
prompt: How does the price elasticity of demand determine whether raising a price increases or decreases total revenue?
answer: Elasticity is the percent change in quantity demanded per one percent change in price. When demand is inelastic, quantity barely falls, so a higher price raises revenue; when demand is elastic, quantity falls sharply, so a higher price lowers revenue.

title: The cost the price leaves out
body: An externality is a cost or benefit landing on someone who was not party to a transaction. A factory that pollutes imposes cleanup and health costs on neighbors, but those costs never enter its price, so it produces more than is socially efficient. A vaccine protects others too, and its private buyer ignores that benefit, so the market underprovides it. Prices coordinate well only when they capture all the costs and benefits.
prompt: Why does a polluting factory produce too much, and a vaccine too little, without anyone behaving irrationally?
answer: An externality is a cost or benefit falling on a third party outside the transaction, so the market price omits it. Markets overproduce goods with negative externalities like pollution and underproduce those with positive externalities like vaccination, because buyers and sellers ignore the effects on others.

title: Why markets underfund the lighthouse
body: A public good is both non-excludable, meaning you cannot easily stop non-payers from using it, and non-rivalrous, meaning one person's use does not diminish another's. National defense and a lighthouse fit: everyone benefits whether or not they paid. That invites free-riding, since each person hopes others foot the bill, so voluntary contributions fall short and the market underprovides the good.
prompt: Why do private markets tend to underprovide public goods like national defense?
answer: A public good is non-excludable and non-rivalrous, so people can benefit without paying and one person's use does not reduce another's. That lets everyone free-ride in hope others will pay, so voluntary provision falls short, which is why such goods are typically funded through taxation.

title: A raise into a higher bracket still pays
body: A common fear is that earning more can push you into a higher tax bracket and leave you with less money. Under a progressive system with marginal rates, that cannot happen from the brackets alone. A bracket's rate applies only to income falling within that bracket, not to your whole income. Cross into the 22% band and only the dollars above the threshold are taxed at 22%. Everything below keeps its lower rates.
prompt: Why can't moving into a higher tax bracket ever leave you with less take-home pay, in a progressive system?
answer: A bracket's rate applies only to the income that falls inside that bracket, not to your entire income, so income below the threshold keeps its lower rates. Extra earnings are therefore never fully clawed back, and your effective rate always stays below your top marginal rate.

title: Who really pays a tax
body: Whether a tax is legally collected from the buyer or the seller barely matters to who ultimately bears it. What decides the burden is the relative elasticity of supply and demand. The more inelastic side, the one less able to walk away, absorbs more of the tax. Tax cigarettes, whose buyers are addicted and unresponsive to price, and consumers pay most of it regardless of who writes the cheque.
prompt: Does it matter whether a tax is legally charged to buyers or to sellers, and what actually decides who bears it?
answer: The legal side that remits the tax barely affects the real burden; what matters is the relative elasticity of supply and demand. The more inelastic side, less able to change its behavior, bears more of the tax regardless of who writes the cheque.

title: Trades a tax quietly kills
body: Beyond the revenue it raises, a tax destroys value by preventing trades that would have benefited both parties. If a job is worth $100 to a buyer and costs a seller $70, they should trade, but a $50 tax wedges apart what the buyer pays and what the seller keeps, and the deal collapses. Nobody captures that lost surplus. It vanishes.
prompt: What is the deadweight loss of a tax, and why is it a cost beyond the revenue collected?
answer: Deadweight loss is the value of mutually beneficial trades that no longer happen because the tax drives a wedge between the price the buyer pays and the price the seller receives. That surplus is captured by no one and simply vanishes. Price controls and monopolies create the same loss.

title: Why the same asset can fetch less in a hurry
body: Liquidity is how easily you can convert an asset to cash quickly without moving its price. A blue-chip stock is liquid, since you can sell instantly at the quoted price. A house or a thinly traded bond is illiquid, so to sell fast you must accept a discount. Because investors dislike being stuck, they demand extra expected return to hold illiquid assets.
prompt: Two assets promise identical cash flows, yet one trades at a lower price. What can explain the gap?
answer: One is harder to get out of. Liquidity is how quickly an asset can be sold for cash without moving its price, and illiquid assets can only be sold fast at a discount. Investors therefore demand a liquidity premium to hold them, which shows up as a lower price for otherwise identical cash flows.

title: What a Big Mac says about exchange rates
body: Purchasing power parity starts from the law of one price: absent trade barriers, the same good should cost the same everywhere once you convert currencies. If a basket of goods is much cheaper in one country, its currency looks undervalued, and PPP says exchange rates should drift to close the gap. The Economist's Big Mac Index makes this playful by using one good, a burger, to compare currencies. Real rates deviate for many reasons.
prompt: What does purchasing power parity claim about exchange rates, and how does the Big Mac Index illustrate it?
answer: Purchasing power parity says exchange rates should move so that a basket of goods costs the same across countries, following the law of one price. The Big Mac Index applies this to a single good, using burger prices to flag currencies that look over- or under-valued, though it holds only as a long-run tendency.

title: Mistaking the number for the value
body: Money illusion is the tendency to think in nominal dollars rather than real, inflation-adjusted ones. A worker given a 2% raise when prices rose 4% feels richer but can actually buy less. People often prefer a small nominal raise in high inflation to a nominal pay cut in zero inflation, even when the second leaves them better off in real terms.
prompt: A colleague celebrates a 2% raise in a year when prices rose 4%. What has she got wrong?
answer: Money illusion is the tendency to reason in nominal rather than real, inflation-adjusted terms. A 2% raise when prices rise 4% looks like a gain but reduces real purchasing power, because people mistake the face value of money for what it can actually buy.

title: Return means little without its risk
body: A fund that returned 20% is not obviously better than one that returned 12%. You have to ask how much risk each took to get there. The Sharpe ratio makes the comparison by taking an investment's return above the risk-free rate and dividing by the volatility of its returns. Two portfolios with the same return can score very differently.
prompt: Why is a raw return figure incomplete, and what does the Sharpe ratio add?
answer: A return says nothing about the risk taken to earn it, so a high return from wild swings may be worse than a steadier lower one. The Sharpe ratio divides return above the risk-free rate by the volatility of returns, measuring reward earned per unit of risk.

title: When money burns faster than a pocket
body: Hyperinflation is inflation so rapid that prices can double in days. Historically it traces to one cause above all: a government financing its deficits by creating money on a vast scale. As the currency loses value by the hour, people refuse to hold it and spend the moment they are paid, which speeds money through the economy and drives prices up further. The spiral feeds itself.
prompt: What typically causes hyperinflation, and why does it tend to accelerate once it starts?
answer: Hyperinflation almost always stems from a government financing deficits by creating money on a large scale. As the currency loses value people spend it immediately rather than hold it, speeding money through the economy and pushing prices up further, a self-feeding spiral that ends only when the money creation stops.

title: The grade that sets the interest rate
body: A credit rating is an estimate of how likely a borrower is to repay, on a scale from top grade down to speculative junk. It forecasts default risk rather than guaranteeing anything. Because lenders demand compensation for risk, a lower rating forces a borrower to pay a higher interest rate, and the extra yield over a safe benchmark is the credit spread.
prompt: What does a credit rating represent, and how does it affect what a borrower pays?
answer: A credit rating forecasts a borrower's likelihood of repaying rather than defaulting, from top grade down to speculative junk. Lower-rated borrowers must pay higher interest to compensate lenders for the added risk, so a downgrade can raise borrowing costs, with the gap over a safe benchmark being the credit spread.

title: The pasture everyone ruins
body: A hundred herders share one open pasture that can sustain a fixed number of animals. Each herder reasons that adding one more cow brings them the full profit of that animal, while the cost of slightly overgrazing is spread across all hundred. So every herder adds cows, the pasture is stripped bare, and all of them end up worse off than if the herd had been capped. Each acted rationally in their own interest.
prompt: Why do herders sharing an open pasture overgraze it into ruin even though each is acting rationally?
answer: Each herder captures the full benefit of an added animal but shares the cost of overgrazing with everyone, so the private calculation always favors adding more. Because all face the same incentive the shared resource is depleted; the fix requires limiting access or making each bear the true social cost.

title: Two confessions nobody wanted
body: Two suspects are held separately and each offered a deal. Stay silent and, if the other also stays silent, both get a light sentence. Betray the other and you go free while they take the heavy fall, unless they betray too, in which case you both get a moderately harsh term. Whatever the other does, betraying leaves you individually better off.
prompt: In the prisoner's dilemma, why do two rational suspects both betray each other and end up worse than if both stayed silent?
answer: Whatever the other does, betraying yields a better individual payoff, so defection is each player's dominant strategy. Both defect and reach the only stable outcome, which is worse for both than mutual cooperation; individual rationality and collective benefit pull apart.

title: The auction you win by losing less
body: A dollar is auctioned to the highest bidder, with a twist: the second-highest bidder also pays their final bid and gets nothing. Bidding starts cheap, since who would not offer five cents for a dollar? As bids near a dollar, the runner-up faces losing their bid outright, so bidding a little more to win looks better than dropping out. Two rational players can end up paying well over a dollar each.
prompt: In the dollar auction, why do rational bidders end up paying more than a dollar for a dollar?
answer: Because the second-highest bidder also forfeits their bid, each player near a dollar faces a certain loss from quitting versus a slightly larger bid that might still win. Raising to avoid the loss always looks better locally, so the two escalate past a dollar, each throwing good money after bad.

title: Why water is cheap and diamonds are dear
body: Water keeps you alive. Diamonds are ornaments you could live without. Yet water costs almost nothing and diamonds cost a fortune. If price tracked usefulness, this ordering would be backwards. Classical economists were stuck on it for a long time, because they kept looking at the total usefulness of each good. The resolution comes from asking a different question: not how useful water is in total, but what you would pay for one more glass.
prompt: Why does water, essential for life, cost far less than diamonds, which are inessential?
answer: Price reflects marginal utility, the value of one more unit, not total usefulness. Water is so abundant that an extra unit is worth almost nothing, while diamonds are scarce so an extra one is highly valued, which reverses the ordering that total usefulness alone would suggest.

title: The certainty people won't give up
body: Choose between A, a guaranteed $1 million, and B, a 10% shot at $5 million, an 89% shot at $1 million, and a 1% shot at nothing. Most people take the sure million. Now choose between C, an 11% chance of $1 million, and D, a 10% chance of $5 million. Most people take D. Examined together, these two choices are inconsistent under any steady valuation of money.
prompt: Why is preferring a sure $1 million in one gamble but the riskier option in a parallel gamble inconsistent?
answer: The two choice pairs differ only by an identical 89% chance of $1 million added to both options, which should cancel out and not flip the preference. Preferring certainty in the first but the higher prize in the second violates the independence axiom of expected utility; people overweight certainty itself.

title: A bet avoided because the odds are hidden
body: An urn holds 90 balls. Exactly 30 are red, and the other 60 are an unknown mix of black and yellow. You can bet on red, a known one-in-three chance, or on black, whose chance is unknown but could reach two-thirds. Most people bet on red. Offered instead a bet on red-or-yellow versus black-or-yellow, most switch to the black side.
prompt: In the Ellsberg urn, why is preferring the known-odds bet in one framing but the unknown-odds bet in another inconsistent?
answer: Preferring red over black implies you treat black as scarce, yet preferring black-or-yellow over red-or-yellow implies you treat black as plentiful, and no single belief about the black count supports both. People are exhibiting ambiguity aversion, favoring known probabilities over unknown ones even at a cost.

title: Active management is arithmetic before it is skill
body: All the shares in a market are held by someone, so the holdings of active investors together are the market minus the holdings of index investors. Before costs, the average actively managed dollar must therefore earn exactly the market return. After costs it must earn less, because active management charges more in fees and trading. William Sharpe made this point without any assumption about market efficiency or investor skill. It follows from adding up.
prompt: What does the average actively managed dollar earn compared with the market, and why does the argument need no view on skill?
answer: Exactly the market return before costs, and less after them. Active and passive holdings together are the whole market, so the active average is the market average by arithmetic, and higher fees and trading costs then subtract from it. Skill and market efficiency never enter the argument.

title: The trade whose losses have no ceiling
body: A short seller borrows shares, sells them, and hopes to buy them back cheaper. Buying a share risks the price falling to zero, so the loss is capped at what you paid. Shorting inverts the payoff, because the price can rise without limit. Worse, a rising price forces margin calls and buying to close, which pushes the price up further.
prompt: Buying a share can cost you everything you put in. What is different about the downside of shorting one?
answer: It has no ceiling. A share price cannot fall below zero, so a buyer's loss is capped at the purchase price, but it can rise without limit, so a short seller's loss is unbounded. Rising prices also trigger margin calls that force buying to close, pushing prices higher still, which is a short squeeze.

title: Why pooling risk makes it smaller
body: An insurer cannot predict whether your house burns down, and does not need to. Pooling many largely independent risks leaves the total loss far more predictable in proportion, because independent variations partly cancel while the average stays put. That is why premiums can be set close to expected losses plus a modest margin. The model breaks when risks are correlated rather than independent, which is why flood and earthquake cover is priced and reinsured very differently.
prompt: An insurer cannot predict any single claim, yet prices policies confidently. What makes the aggregate easier than the individual?
answer: Pooling many largely independent risks makes the total loss proportionally far more predictable, since independent variations partly cancel out while the average holds. The reasoning fails when risks are correlated, as with floods or earthquakes, where one event hits the whole pool at once.

title: What GDP was never built to measure
body: GDP totals the market value of goods and services produced in a period. It therefore counts a traffic jam's petrol and a hurricane's rebuilding as output, while unpaid childcare, household work and leisure contribute nothing. It is silent on how the total is distributed and on depletion of natural capital. Simon Kuznets, who built the US accounts, warned in 1934 that national welfare could scarcely be inferred from them.
prompt: GDP rises after a hurricane and ignores unpaid childcare entirely. Is that a flaw in the statistic?
answer: No, it is the definition working as intended. GDP measures the market value of production in a period, so rebuilding counts and unpriced household work does not. It was never designed to capture welfare, distribution, or the depletion of natural capital, a limit Kuznets stated when he built the accounts.

title: Three policies, and you may have two
body: A country cannot simultaneously hold a fixed exchange rate, allow free movement of capital, and run an independent monetary policy. Cut rates below the anchor country's and capital leaves in search of yield, which forces the currency down unless you defend the peg until reserves run out. Pick any two and the third must give. Hong Kong keeps the peg and open capital and imports US policy; most large economies float instead.
prompt: A central bank wants a currency peg, open capital markets, and rates set for its own economy. Which can it have?
answer: Any two of the three, never all of them, a constraint known as the impossible trinity. Setting rates independently under open capital flows moves capital in or out until the peg breaks or reserves are exhausted, so a country either floats, closes its capital account, or accepts the anchor country's policy.

title: The funds that are no longer in the table
body: A table of fund returns over twenty years lists funds that still exist. Poor performers were closed or merged into better ones along the way, and their records left with them. The surviving sample therefore reports a return well above what an investor choosing at the start would have earned. Studies putting the gap at roughly one percentage point a year are common, which is enough to change the ranking against an index.
prompt: Why does a twenty-year table of fund returns overstate what an investor would actually have earned?
answer: Because it only lists funds that survived. Poor performers were closed or merged away and their records left the sample, so the reported average reflects survivors rather than the full set an investor could have picked at the start. The gap is commonly estimated at around a percentage point a year.

title: One percent, compounded for thirty years
body: A fee sounds small next to a return, but it is charged on the whole balance every year, and the money it removes stops compounding. Invest £10,000 for thirty years at 7%, and you finish with about £76,100. Charge 1% a year and the effective return is 6%, leaving about £57,400. The extra quarter of the balance did not vanish into one year's fee. It is thirty years of growth that never happened.
prompt: A 1% annual fee against a 7% return sounds like a small bite. What does it cost over thirty years?
answer: Roughly a quarter of the final balance. £10,000 at 7% for thirty years grows to about £76,100, while the same sum at 6% reaches about £57,400. The loss is not the fee itself but the compounding on every pound the fee removed along the way.

title: Two ways a bank dies, and two different cures
body: A bank fails for one of two reasons. It is insolvent when its assets are worth less than what it owes, and it is illiquid when the assets are fine but cannot be turned into cash fast enough. Capital, meaning equity funding rather than debt, absorbs losses and addresses the first. Liquid asset buffers and central bank lending address the second. The distinction matters because lending to an insolvent bank only enlarges the eventual loss.
prompt: A bank with sound loans and a bank with bad loans both cannot pay depositors today. Why do they need different remedies?
answer: One is illiquid and one is insolvent. Illiquidity means good assets that cannot be converted to cash quickly, which liquid buffers or central bank lending against collateral can bridge. Insolvency means the assets are worth less than the liabilities, which only more capital resolves, and lending to an insolvent bank enlarges the eventual loss.

title: Goods people buy more of as they get dearer
body: Demand curves usually slope downward, but two exceptions run the other way for different reasons. A Veblen good is bought partly because it is expensive, so a higher price raises its appeal directly. A Giffen good is a staple so dominant in a poor household's budget that a price rise leaves them too poor to afford anything better, forcing them to buy more of it. Veblen goods are easy to observe, whereas convincing empirical Giffen cases are rare.
prompt: Two kinds of good see demand rise when the price does. What separates them?
answer: The mechanism. A Veblen good is desired partly for its expense, so price feeds demand directly through status, whereas a Giffen good is a cheap staple whose price rise makes a poor household so much worse off that they drop costlier foods and eat more of the staple. Veblen effects are readily observed, while empirical Giffen cases are rare and contested.

title: Who pockets a housing subsidy
body: Give renters a monthly housing subsidy and their willingness to pay rises by roughly that amount. Where new housing can be built quickly, supply expands and most of the benefit reaches tenants. Where building is constrained by planning rules or geography, quantity cannot respond, so the extra demand shows up almost entirely in rents and the landlord captures much of the money. The intended recipient of a transfer and its eventual beneficiary are decided by elasticities.
prompt: A city introduces a rent subsidy for tenants. What determines whether tenants or landlords end up with the money?
answer: How elastic housing supply is. Where new building responds quickly, quantity rises and most of the subsidy reaches tenants. Where supply is fixed by planning limits or geography, the extra demand raises rents instead, and landlords capture much of the transfer.
